Choose the Hyperparameters by Cross-Validation

Source: R/path.R
cv.Rd

Builds the object with which statmod() chooses the hyperparameters of the penalties with a kink by cross-validation: the points of a path of values are scored by the log-likelihood that the fit assigns to observations on which it was not fitted, and the best is kept. The result is passed as sparse_criterion. It is not an outer criterion: outer_criterion = cv() is an error, because the smoothing parameters are estimated by reml(), ml(), aic() or bic().

Usage

cv(nfolds = 10, folds = NULL, rule = c("min", "1se"))

Arguments

nfolds

How many folds, a single number of at least 2. The default is 10. It is ignored when folds is given.

folds

A fold number per observation, an integer vector as long as the data, for a user-defined partition or to compare two criteria on the same one. NULL, the default, draws a partition with a fixed seed.

rule

"min" for the best criterion, "1se" for the sparsest fit within one standard error of it. It is matched with match.arg().

Value

An OuterMethod() object of kind "cv", carrying nfolds, rule and folds. Its hessian is "observed" and its k is NA_real_; this criterion reads neither.

Cross-validation for a penalty with a kink

A marginal criterion, reml() or ml(), approximates an integral by a Laplace expansion at the penalized mode, which requires the second derivative of the penalty there. The mode of a lasso, a SCAD or an MCP sits at the kink for every coefficient that it sets to zero, and the derivative does not exist at the kink, so the criterion is undefined at the point at which it would be read.

Cross-validation scores prediction and not a posterior, and it needs nothing from the penalty beyond a fit.

Passed as sparse_criterion to a model with no hyperparameter of a kinked penalty left to estimate, cv() has no effect.

The criterion

The criterion is the mean over folds of \(-2\ell_f/w_f\), where \(\ell_f\) is the weighted log-likelihood of the fold left out at the coefficients fitted on the other folds, and \(w_f\) is the sum of the weights of its rows. Each training fit reapplies to its rows the terms built on all the rows (knots, factor levels and scales of standardization), as predict.StatmodFit() does for new data, and carries the weights and offsets of the fit.

rule = "1se" takes the largest kink whose criterion is within one standard error of the smallest, which is the sparsest fit that is not measurably worse.

The folds

Unless folds is given, the observations are assigned to folds by a permutation drawn with a fixed seed, and the caller's random-number state is restored afterwards, so that the partition does not depend on the caller's seed.

The path

The penalized mode is a piecewise smooth function of the hyperparameter: differentiable while the active set holds, turning a corner whenever a coefficient joins it or leaves. A criterion read there inherits the corners, so a gradient search would read a slope about to change.

The hyperparameter is therefore swept over a grid, geometric in the size of the kink, from the value that leaves the block empty down to min_ratio of it. Every fit starts from the previous one's coefficients.

Which hyperparameters

The path covers every hyperparameter of the term's penalty that the constructor did not hold at a number.

A product within a term, an alternation between terms

For a term with several kinked hyperparameters, every combination is visited under search = "grid" and one hyperparameter is swept at a time under "cyclic".

The choice belongs to the term, through enet(X, search =) and modelterms7::term_search(), and not to this criterion. The criterion is also applied to the model's smooth hyperparameters, which are read at the mode and not swept, so that an argument of this kind would have no meaning for them.

Between two terms the sweep alternates whichever search each one names, so that y ~ lasso(X) + enet(R) costs the two blocks added and not multiplied, and a term that sets a product does not make the other term pay for it.

A term that names neither is swept over the product, because the cyclic sweep traverses a cross through the point in hand and can stop where each coordinate is separately best without being jointly so. Its cost is the product of the term's grids, whereas the cost of the cyclic sweep is their sum. At two hyperparameters this is n_lambda * n_alpha fits against n_lambda + n_alpha per pass. If three or more hyperparameters are estimated, the cost of the product grows exponentially, and "cyclic" is there for that case.

How long the path is, and how far down it reaches

The length of the path and its depth are settings of the term, written on its own signature: lasso(x, n_lambda = 25, min_ratio = 1e-4) and enet(x, n_lambda = 25, n_alpha = 5).

The two numbers differ because the axes do. \(\lambda\) descends the size of the kink over four decades, while \(\alpha\) spans one bounded interval, so that the default product is 25 by 5.

The shape of the grid

The grid is not a rectangle for the elastic net and is a rectangle for SCAD and MCP. The elastic net's kink is \(\lambda\alpha\), so the value emptying the block is \(\lambda_{\max} = \kappa/\alpha\) and every \(\alpha\) carries its own \(\lambda\) axis, descending from its own top. The shapes of SCAD and MCP do not change the kink, so that \(\lambda_{\max}\) is one number whatever the shape and the two axes form a rectangle. Each axis is built at the settings of the axes outside it, which covers both cases without a rule about families.

The cost

Each point of the path costs nfolds fits. The number of points is the term's n_lambda for one kinked hyperparameter, and the product of its axes for several. The fits along a path are warm-started within each fold.

The folds run over separate R processes when statmod(threads = n_threads(workers = 4)) requests them. One seed is drawn per fold in the parent, so that the answer is identical at any worker count.

References

Breiman, L., Friedman, J. H., Olshen, R. A. and Stone, C. J. (1984). Classification and Regression Trees. Wadsworth.

Friedman, J., Hastie, T. and Tibshirani, R. (2010). Regularization paths for generalized linear models via coordinate descent. Journal of Statistical Software 33(1), 1–22.

See also

aic() and bic() for the other prediction-error criteria, reml() for the marginal ones, statmod() for where this is passed, hyper() for reading back what it chose.

Examples

# Two of eight columns carry signal; the rest are noise for the path to
# shrink away.
set.seed(1)
X <- matrix(rnorm(120 * 8), 120, 8)
dd <- data.frame(y = 1 + X %*% c(2, -1.5, rep(0, 6)) + rnorm(120, sd = 0.5))
dd$x <- X

fit <- statmod(y ~ lasso(x, n_lambda = 12),
               distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), dd,
               sparse_criterion = cv(nfolds = 5))
hyper(fit)
#>   parameter                    term   name estimate  held source   id
#> 1        mu lasso(x, n_lambda = 12) lambda 14.03983 FALSE     cv <NA>

# The two columns that carry signal are recovered.
round(coef(fit)$mu[2:3], 3)
#> lasso.1 lasso.2 
#>   1.995  -1.512 

# "1se" takes the largest kink within one standard error of the best, so
# it never keeps more coefficients than "min". On this data the two agree,
# because the only sparser point of the path has a criterion more than one
# standard error above the minimum.
one_se <- statmod(y ~ lasso(x, n_lambda = 12),
                  distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), dd,
                  sparse_criterion = cv(nfolds = 5, rule = "1se"))
c(min = hyper(fit)$estimate, one_se = hyper(one_se)$estimate)
#>      min   one_se 
#> 14.03983 14.03983 
c(min = sum(coef(fit)$mu[-1] != 0), one_se = sum(coef(one_se)$mu[-1] != 0))
#>    min one_se 
#>      7      7
